transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-26 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Anika Bose (Redwood Product), Sofia Martinez (Aurelia), Ethan Wu (Aurelia Eng Mgr), Priya Nair (Aurelia SRE), Liam O'Connor (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming generation basics, parameter tuning (temp, top_p, max_tokens), and resiliency strategies (retries, fallbacks). Showed Redwood Console cost/latency breakdown and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer raised latency SLO (<=200ms p95), data residency/KMS questions, and interest in a short pilot. Next steps captured.

Topics:
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options for latency and compliance
- Streaming behavior and SDK patterns (idempotency keys, backoff)
- Gen params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop tokens, streaming chunk sizes
- Optimize recommendations: batching, prefix caching, quantization profiles
- Console: token-level cost, per-route dashboards, rollout controls

Action items (captured above): see action_items field.

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood hosted team. Quick intros?
[00:12] Sofia (Aurelia): Hi, Sofia here, product lead for our customer chat product.
[00:18] Ethan (Aurelia): Ethan, engineering manager, focused on latency and infra.
[00:23] Priya (Aurelia): Priya, SRE, I care about security, KMS, and audit logs.
[00:28] Maya: Great — Carlos will run the demo and I'll cover pricing/next steps.
[00:34] Carlos (Redwood SE): Hey all, I'll share my screen. Quick note on agenda: streaming demo, parameters, retries and then Console + Optimize tour.
[00:43] Liam (Aurelia): We're particularly interested in tail latency and cost per 1k tokens, plus control plane for audits.
[00:51] Carlos: Totally. Quick qual — what's your current stack for chat? Are you using a vector DB or RAG pattern?
[01:00] Sofia: We use an internal RAG stack with Pinecone right now; it's alpha. Typical prompt sizes are 600–900 tokens including history. Peak QPS ~25, sustained ~5.
[01:12] Ethan: Our SLO is 200ms p95 for short replies (<150 tokens). For longer, we can accept more.
[01:20] Carlos: Good context — so prefix/K-V cache reuse will be useful. We demo how Redwood keeps KV cache warm to avoid repeated KV rewarm.
[01:29] Maya: On the compliance side, Priya had questions about KMS and data residency?
[01:35] Priya: Yes — we need customer-managed keys and audit trails, plus SOC2 evidence. Also on-prem or VPC option might be needed for regs.
[01:44] Maya: We can provide KMS/HSM integrations and a Private deployment. We'll attach the security pack after.
[01:50] Carlos: Starting the streaming example — here's a basic chat generation call to the hosted endpoint.
[02:00] [screen-share noise] Carlos: I'm calling /v1/chat/completions with stream:true. As tokens arrive you can see the socket emit delta events.
[02:12] Carlos: Note — streaming chunk size is influenced by model and max_tokens, and the SDK exposes a stream handler so you can render partials.
[02:23] Sofia: If a stream drops mid-response what's the recommended client behavior?
[02:27] Carlos: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys per user-turn, short exponential backoff with jitter, and fallback to a synchronous re-request or smaller model. Also persist partials when appropriate so UI can show last good chunk.
[02:41] Ethan: What about duplicate tokens if we retry?
[02:44] Carlos: Use idempotency and token offsets — our SDK handles de-dup on the same request id if you pass the same key. If you reissue without key you'll risk duplicates.
[02:54] [00:02:54 ambient noise]
[03:05] Carlos: Now parameters: temperature controls randomness; temp 0.0–0.2 for deterministic, 0.7–1.0 for creative. top_p as nucleus sampling — you can tune instead of temp.
[03:18] Carlos: max_tokens caps length; presence_penalty and frequency_penalty help reduce repetition. We show a live toggle of temp and top_p and regen.
[03:30] Sofia: For our use case we want guardrails, so deterministic mostly. Also we have stop tokens for truncation.
[03:38] Carlos: Right, stop sequences reduce token usage and cost. Also you can stream with partial stop-handling client-side.
[03:46] Carlos: On retries — we recommend exponential backoff with max attempts 3 for transient 5xx and network errors. For 4xx like rate-limit you should surface to user or retry after Retry-After.
[03:58] Anika (Product): We also support automatic fallback policies at the routing layer — route to a cheaper quantized variant or a smaller model when latency spikes.
[04:08] Ethan: How transparent is the fallback in the response? Will we know which variant served the request?
[04:12] Carlos: Yes — we include model metadata and routing reason in the response headers and Console logs.
[04:20] [04:20] Carlos: Switching to Console — here is per-route latency, token cost breakdown, and traces.
[04:30] [04:30] Carlos: You can filter by model, key, and route. Token-level cost shows prompt vs completion tokens so you can optimize prompts.
[04:40] Priya: Can we get token-cost at log-level for audit?
[04:43] Carlos: Yes, Console retains token-level breakdowns and you can export CSVs or send to SIEM.
[04:49] Carlos: Now Optimize — it analyzes your workload and suggests batching sizes, quantization profiles, and cache TTLs.
[04:57] Carlos: For example, for short replies the tool recommended dynamic batching of 8 with a 20ms aggregation window which preserved p95 and reduced per-token CPU.
[05:09] Ethan: Does Optimize give confidence estimates?
[05:12] Carlos: It includes expected latency and cost delta ranges — these are heuristics from prior runs so treat as guidance, we recommend running a short pilot.
[05:21] Sofia: Could you show quantization tradeoffs?
[05:24] Carlos: Sure — here's a comparison: int8 quant reduces memory and cost, small quality difference in our eval on chat prompts; 4-bit quant can be aggressive. We recommend model-specific profiles and the Console flags to test in canary.
[05:40] [05:40] Carlos: Moving to resilience patterns: automatic canaries, A/B rollouts, and automatic fallback to a smaller variant are available. For mission-critical you might want Dedicated capacity.
[05:52] Maya: Quick pricing note — hosted per-token units with burst capacity add-on; Dedicated is committed monthly with reserved GPU pools. We'll email a side-by-side.
[06:05] Liam: For Dedicated, can we reserve capacity in a region for data residency?
[06:09] Carlos: Yes, Dedicated or Private lets you pin region, and Private has on-prem options if needed.
[06:15] Priya: KMS? Do you support customer-managed keys?
[06:18] Maya: Yes, integration with major cloud KMS and HSM options for Private. We'll include the integration guides.
[06:25] Carlos: Now a small perf test — I'm running 50 simulated requests with one model and showing p95. (Shows chart)
[06:33] Carlos: You can see warm KV-cache drops median latency significantly.
[06:38] Ethan: What's the expected warm-up cost/time for KV caches?
[06:42] Carlos: Depends on prompt size; for typical 600 token context it can be a few hundred ms cold, but with continuous batching and reuse it stabilizes. Using prefix caching we saw p95 drop by ~150–200ms in our internal examples.
[06:55] Sofia: Do we need to modify our RAG to use prefix caching?
[06:58] Carlos: Minimal changes — the SDK exposes cache hints; you can provide conversation ids so we reuse KV for a session.
[07:06] [07:06] Priya: On audit logs, do you retain raw inputs? We need redaction for PII.
[07:11] Maya: You control retention and can enable token redaction; audit trails will show metadata for each request without payload if desired. We'll include the retention config doc.
[07:20] Carlos: Back to retries — for streaming we recommend snapshotting partial responses on client and then re-requesting with same idempotency key and an instruction to continue from token offset.
[07:34] Ethan: That sounds heavy — is there SDK help?
[07:37] Carlos: Yes our SDK has helpers for reconciling partials and rehydrating streams; sample code will be in the demo repo.
[07:45] [07:45] Sofia: About cost — can Optimize point to prompt-level changes that reduce tokens?
[07:50] Anika: Yes, Optimize flags high token prompts and suggests compression techniques and prompt trimming. It pairs with Console so you can see before/after cost delta in a canary run.
[08:02] Carlos: Live Q&A:
[08:05] Liam: If we hit a region outage, how do you failover?
[08:09] Carlos: Smart routing can failover to other regions and compatible model variants; for strict data residency we do not automatically cross borders unless policy allows.
[08:20] Priya: Good. Also timeline — we are aiming to pilot next month. What's required to start?
[08:26] Maya: Minimal: sign basic terms, provide traffic profile, and we spin up a pilot org with dev keys and a perf script. SE (Carlos) will lead perf.
[08:35] Ethan: For the pilot, can we run a concurrency test with our typical prompts?
[08:39] Carlos: Absolutely — send sample payloads and we'll run the script.
[08:43] [08:43] Maya: Another question from Sofia: safety / toxicity filtering?
[08:47] Carlos: Redwood supports safety filters and you can add post-processing or rerankers; we can show the safety settings in Console.
[08:54] Sofia: Great.
[08:56] [08:56 to 18:00 omitted — long demo running through Console dashboards and Optimize suggestions, chatty screen-share commentary with minor transcription gaps]
[18:05] Carlos: Jumping back — one advanced tip: use smaller context windows for shorter queries and separate long-term context into embeddings + RAG so you avoid hot KV for every request.
[18:18] Ethan: Makes sense. For our 600–900 token context maybe split static persona + recent messages.
[18:25] Carlos: Exactly. Also, turn on prefix caching TTL to retain the heavy tokens for a session length you expect.
[18:33] Sofia: For retries with streaming, if we fall back to non-streaming synchronous it will increase latency — is that acceptable?
[18:39] Maya: It's a tradeoff — better UX to finish a response slowly than show an error. Our recommended pattern: try streaming retry once, then fallback to cached or smaller model.
[18:50] Priya: Are there audit hooks for each retry? We want to know when the system retried.
[18:54] Carlos: Yes, every attempt is logged with attempt number and routing reason.
[18:59] [19:00] Carlos: Quick note about rate-limits — we have tiered limits and per-key quotas. For pilots we usually bump limits.
[19:08] Ethan: Ok. Any gotchas with stop tokens and streaming?
[19:12] Carlos: If a stop token is emitted mid-chunk, client should respect it but you may get a trailing token in the next chunk; SDK normalizes.
[19:21] Sofia: How do we measure quality regressions across model upgrades?
[19:25] Anika: Console has eval sets and regression alerts tied to prompt sets — you can pin model versions and set rollbacks on quality drops.
[19:35] Liam: Excellent.
[19:38] [19:38] Maya: Recap and next steps: I'll send pricing and security pack; Carlos will share perf script and demo repo; Ethan and Priya will send traffic profile and KMS/region constraints.
[19:50] Sofia: Sounds good. One last quick question: is there a built-in client-side debounce for streaming UI to avoid many re-renders?
[19:58] Carlos: Client-side not in Redwood but our SDK has a stream consumer that batches delta events; front-end sample shows a 50ms throttle.
[20:08] Maya: We're at ~20 minutes in the demo window — any final items?
[20:12] Priya: No; just confirm you'll include the SOC2 report and retention options.
[20:16] Maya: Yes.
[20:18] Ethan: We'll aim to get sample payloads by Friday.
[20:21] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
[20:26] Carlos: Thanks everyone.
[20:29] [20:29] Call ends — informal wrap, credit card noise.

Notes about transcript quality: Some technical terms transcribed imperfectly (K-V cache sometimes as K-V cash, quantization as quantize-shun), model names redacted in the demo for disclosure.

End of transcript.
